## Findings, most severe first

### 1. The issues badge brings back both symptoms as soon as anything logs an error (dev-only, medium)

`devIndicators: false` removes the idle badge, but Next's issues badge still renders on the first logged error, and it is focusable. This application logs one itself — `console.error("Chat request failed:", error)` in `settleWithError`, `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/apps/web/src/components/chat.tsx:427` — so it fires on the **first chat send against a stack with no chat service**, which is this stack and is the journey under review.

Measured at 1440×900, panel reopened after one failed send, tabbing from `#chat`:

```
1. BUTTON  Send message            shadow=0  dialog=1
2. BUTTON  Close chat              shadow=0  dialog=1
3. BUTTON  Open issues overlay     shadow=1  dialog=0   <- closes a keystroke early
4. BUTTON  Collapse issues badge   shadow=1  dialog=0
5. BODY
```

That is your "indicator on" column reproduced after the change — two dev stops instead of one, same mechanism (portal after the widget), same early close.

At 390×844 the badge renders at `{x:28, y:790, w:61, h:32}` over the input at `{x:12, y:788, w:310, h:44}`: `elementFromPoint` at 5%, 15% and 30% of the input width returns `NEXTJS-PORTAL`, and the placeholder reads "…roduct…" behind a red "1 Issue ×" pill. Pointer taps on the input's left third hit the badge. Evidence: `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-contoso/32326432-9961-4c06-ab5c-44ff606dccde/scratchpad/shots/phone-error-badge.png`. At 1440×900 the badge sits bottom-left and overlaps nothing (`overlapCount: 0`).

Nothing here reaches production — the overlay portal is dev-only, and the config comment already says errors still surface. What is wrong is the scope of the two claims built on it: the tab-order guarantee and the 390 clearance both hold only until the app logs its first error. Suggested fix: qualify the comment in `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/apps/web/next.config.js` (and #277) to say the badge returns on error, and review keyboard journeys that must match production against `next start` rather than `next dev`. A silent error state is not a state a review can rely on.

### 2. At 390×844 the launcher and Send occupy the identical spot (low, pre-existing)

Launcher `{x:334, y:788, w:40, h:40}`; after opening, Send is `{x:334, y:788, w:44, h:44}` — same origin. The pointer that opened the sheet is left over Send, measurable as its hover fill (sky-800 `lab(35.16 -9.58 -34.41)` rather than the resting sky-700 `lab(41.60 -9.11 -42.56)` seen at desktop). Harm is small because an empty send is a no-op, but the comment at `chat.tsx:530-538` presents the crowding as resolved by moving Close into the header; the collision with Send survived it. Suggested fix: nudge the sheet's input row or the launcher so the two do not share an origin.

### 3. Header controls in the sheet are 36×36 (low)

Clear conversation and Close chat measure 36×36 at 390×844; the desktop launcher is 40×40. Passes WCAG 2.5.8 (24px) and fails 2.5.5 (44px) — which the Send button in the same row deliberately meets at 44×44. Inconsistent rather than broken.

## Checks that passed

- **Focus:** moves to `#chat` on open at both viewports. Escape closes and returns focus to the launcher — measured both from a control and from a non-control node inside the panel. Resize across `lg` with the panel open keeps focus in the widget (`INPUT/Message`) and flips `aria-modal`, `inert` and `body.overflow` together in both directions.
- **Keyboard journey:** completable without a mouse. Enter sends, clears the field, leaves focus on the input, appends the turn.
- **Modal contract:** 390 and 834 → `aria-modal="true"`, 1 inert sibling, `body.overflow: hidden`, sheet fills the viewport (390×844, 834×1112), sheet-only `h2 "Chat with Jane Doe"`. 1440 → no `aria-modal`, no inert, no trap, card 650×788. Trap wraps in both directions below `lg`; no trap above it.
- **Contrast (computed against the real white panel):** input text 10.44:1; placeholder and resting ring both 4.83:1; focus outline sky-700 5.86:1 (1.4.11 wants 3:1); send fill vs panel 5.86:1 and its white glyph 5.86:1; user bubble text 6.08:1; assistant text and `h2` 17.72:1. All pass AA.
- **Semantics:** `h1` then `h2`s, sheet's `h2` last — no skipped level. Input has `aria-label="Message"`, icons `aria-hidden`, log is `role="log" aria-live="polite"`.
- **Responsiveness / error state:** no horizontal overflow at 390 (`scrollWidth === clientWidth === 390`); the error turn renders legibly and in full ("Sorry, something went wrong. Please try again.").

## Not performed, with reasons

- **The "indicator on" column, directly.** Reproducing it requires setting `devIndicators` back on, which is a repository edit. Corroborated instead by the error badge in finding 1, which is the same portal in the same document position and produces the same table.
- **2× density.** Not applicable — the diff changes `devIndicators` only; no `srcset`, source dimensions or `deviceSizes` entry moved.

> it appears on the first logged error, and this application logs one itself — `console.error` in `chat.tsx`'s `settleWithError`, on any stack with no chat service.

`settleWithError` is the `.catch` arm of `send(sendChatMessage(...))`, and `sendChatMessage` does not reject on that path. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/apps/web/src/lib/messaging.ts:159-160` wraps the whole fetch in `try/catch` and **resolves** with an error turn:

```js
} catch (error) {
    console.error("Error sending chat message:", error);
    return { name: "Jane Doe", message: "Sorry, something went wrong. ..." }
```

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/apps/web/src/components/chat.tsx:423` says so in as many words ("sendChatMessage resolves with an error turn rather than rejecting"), and line 444 is the only call site. So on a stack with no chat service the log that lights the issues badge is `messaging.ts:160`, and `settleWithError` never runs.

Scenario in which this produces a wrong result: someone later re-derives this qualification, follows the pointer to `settleWithError`, sees it is unreachable on a chat-service outage, and concludes the qualification is stale — deleting the one sentence that stops a reader believing dev now matches production. Fix: name `sendChatMessage`'s `catch` in `src/lib/messaging.ts`.

### 2. "What is given up" understates the cost and misstates the mechanism — refinement (confidence 80)

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/apps/web/next.config.js:100-106`

Re-derived from Next 16.3's own shipped sources (`apps/web/node_modules/next/dist/compiled/next-devtools/index.js` plus the original TSX recovered from its source map):

- **Scope.** `next-logo.tsx` renders the trigger as `{!state.disableDevIndicator && <button id="next-logo" ref={triggerRef} aria-controls="nextjs-dev-tools-menu">}`. That button is the only way into the menu — `panel-router.tsx` builds Route (`Static`/`Dynamic`), Bundler, Preferences, Segment Explorer and version staleness inside it, and the only shortcut (`state.hideShortcut` → `toggleDevtools`) merely toggles the `display` of an element that is no longer rendered. So what is given up is the whole Dev Tools menu, not "the badge's static/dynamic route marker" — and the marker was never on the badge.
- **Mechanism.** Next's own route-info copy says a path is dynamic when "a Dynamic API or a `fetch` option of `{ cache: 'no-store' }` is discovered". The verdict does not read the database. The `NEXT_BUILD_SKIP_DB=1` hazard in `apps/web/AGENTS.md` is about the *content* a prerender captures, not about a different static/dynamic verdict, so "reads the wrong environment … which has no database where the dev server does" does not hold as stated. The conclusion it supports — that the build output is the instrument — is still right, and `next build --debug` exists in 16.3 (`dist/cli/next-build.js:51`).
- **One qualification the paragraph is missing.** `display: state.disableDevIndicator && (!hasError || dismissed) ? 'none' : 'block'`, and the Collapse button sets `dismissed` with no reset path. With the indicator on, collapsing only un-expands and a new error re-expands; with it off, one click on the X hides the issues badge for the rest of the page session, including for errors that arrive later. "none" : "flex"}`, i.e. the logo hides *so that* the status pill can take its place. So `devIndicators: false` also removes the "compiling" and "rendering" feedback in dev, and the cache badge, neither of which is reachable from the Dev Tools menu.

## Refinement 2 — "Errors still surface with this off" is unconditional, and the dismiss path makes it conditional

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/apps/web/next.config.js:106-113`

Same bundle, same component:

```js

...
let Y = h.disableDevIndicator && (!j || O) ? "none" : "block"
...
!h.buildError && jsx("button", {"data-issues-collapse":!0, "aria-label":"Collapse issues badge",

`j` is `totalErrorCount > 0`. `O` is the dismissed flag, set by the collapse button *only* on the `disableDevIndicator` branch. The only state resync in the component is `R !== j && (P(j), I(j))`, which touches `N`/`R` and never `O`. So `O` is one-way for the life of the mounted component: once the X is clicked, `Y` stays `"none"` for every subsequent error until a full reload.

That matters more than a footnote, because "Errors still surface with this off" is the load-bearing safety claim the rest of the block rests on ("it is also the boundary on everything above"). The claim holds until a developer clicks the X once — after which errors are silent for the rest of the session, and the boundary the comment draws is not there. On the non-disabled path the same click calls `I(!1)`, which *does* get resynced by `R !== j`, so this one-way behaviour is specific to the configuration this change introduces.

`.github/dependabot.yml` puts `eslint-config-next` in the `eslint` group, because the group's `eslint-*` pattern matches it:

detect_changed_surfaces.py has no pattern for .github/dependabot.yml, so it falls back to the full runtime gate

Found by `verifier` while verifying `chore/dependabot-ignore-eslint-major`. Pre-existing, not introduced by that branch.

## Measured

`.github/dependabot.yml` appears in none of `detect_changed_surfaces.py`'s pattern lists -- not `RUNTIME_PATTERNS`, `WEB_PATTERNS`, `CHAT_PATTERNS`, or `DOC_PATTERNS`. Classifying a changeset containing only that file:

```
runtime=True, unknown=True
```

`unknown` force-falls-back to the full runtime recommendation, so a one-line edit to the Dependabot config runs the entire merge gate: web CI, chat CI, the journey smoke, the onboarding smoke.

`git log` shows this file has never been added to any pattern list, so every Dependabot config change in the repository's history has taken the same route.

## Why it is not simply a bug

The fallback is the safe direction. An unrecognised path running too much is the failure mode you want, and it is presumably why the `unknown` branch exists at all.

What is worth deciding is whether this particular file should keep taking it. Two arguments pull against each other:

- **It changes no runtime code.** Nothing it touches can affect a rendered pixel or a served byte. On that reading it belongs with the docs surface, or a narrower gate of its own.
- **It changes what future upgrades look like.** A grouping or `ignore` edit decides which dependency pull requests arrive and how they are bundled -- and dependency upgrades are exactly the thing that *can* move rendering behaviour. On that reading the full gate is not obviously wrong.

There is also a third option: leave the routing alone and add the path to a pattern list purely so the classification is deliberate rather than incidental. Right now the behaviour is correct by accident, and nothing records that anyone chose it.

## Suggested direction

Decide which of the three the repository wants, then either add `.github/dependabot.yml` to a pattern list or write down in `scripts/detect_changed_surfaces.py` why it is deliberately unmatched. A comment naming the choice is worth more than the routing either way, since the current state cannot be told apart from an oversight -- which is how it was found.

- #252 -- the grouping question in the same file.
- #69 -- the upstream ESLint block the hold in that file now records.

Every label dependabot.yml asks for is missing, so no dependency PR has ever been labelled

Found while draining the Dependabot pull request queue.

## Measured

`.github/dependabot.yml` declares four labels across its five update entries:

```
chat
dependencies
github-actions
web
```

`gh label list` returns only the nine GitHub defaults -- `bug`, `documentation`, `duplicate`, `enhancement`, `good first issue`, `help wanted`, `invalid`, `question`, `wontfix`. **None of the four exists.**

Dependabot says so on every pull request it opens. From #226:

> ### Labels
>
> The following labels could not be found: `dependencies`, `web`. Please create them before Dependabot can add them to a pull request.
>
> Please fix the above issues or remove invalid values from `dependabot.yml`.

## Why it has gone unnoticed

The comment is posted on the pull request rather than failing a check, and Dependabot opens the pull request anyway -- just unlabelled. Nothing is red. The `labels:` keys have been in the config since it was written, so there has never been a labelled dependency pull request to contrast against.

The consequence is small but real: `label:dependencies` matches nothing, so there is no way to filter the queue, and the per-ecosystem `web` / `chat` / `github-actions` split the config was clearly designed around does not exist in practice.

1. **Create the four labels.** Makes the committed config work as written. This is a change to the repository's shared label taxonomy, which is why it is filed rather than done.
2. **Delete the `labels:` keys.** Also removes the error comment, and is the honest option if nobody wants the taxonomy.

======== #281 ========
vitest.config.ts warns on every test run and breaks on a future Vite major

Found by `code-review` during #228. Unrelated to that change; it prints on every `make test-web` run today.

## What happens

```
(!) Your Vite config uses features that are unsupported by `configLoader: 'native'`,
    which is planned to become the default in a future major version of Vite:
  - ESM syntax in a file loaded as CommonJS (vitest.config.ts:1:1).
    Use a `.mjs` extension or set "type": "module" in the closest package.json
```

`apps/web/vitest.config.ts` uses `import`/`export default`, and the nearest `package.json` declares no `"type"`, so Node loads it as CommonJS and Vite falls back off the native config loader.

## Why it is worth doing before it has to be

Today it is noise on every test run. It stops being noise when `configLoader: 'native'` becomes the Vite default, at which point the config fails to load rather than warning — so this is a deprecation with a known end date rather than a style preference.

`next dev` prints a matching warning for `apps/web/tailwind.config.ts`, for the same reason:

```
[MODULE_TYPELESS_PACKAGE_JSON] Warning: Module type of .../tailwind.config.ts is not specified
and it doesn't parse as CommonJS. Reparsing as ES module because module syntax was detected.
This incurs a performance overhead.
```

So there are at least two files in `apps/web/` in this state.

## Options

1. Rename to `vitest.config.mts` — smallest blast radius, fixes one file.
2. Add `"type": "module"` to `apps/web/package.json` — fixes both, and every other config file in the directory, but it changes how *every* `.js` file under `apps/web/` is interpreted. `next.config.js` uses `require()` and `module.exports` and would have to become `next.config.cjs` or be converted, and `postcss.config.js` is in the same position. Not a one-line change, and worth checking what else assumes CommonJS before taking it.

Option 1 unblocks the deprecation; option 2 is the tidier end state and needs its own look.

test_agent_definitions only guards agent names below one heading, so names elsewhere in AGENTS.md can go stale

Found by `code-review` while reviewing the AGENTS.md change that adds *Unrelated findings become issues*. Same shape as #100, lower severity, so filing rather than widening a documentation change.

## What is unguarded

`tests/scripts/test_agent_definitions.py` exists so AGENTS.md cannot claim a sub-agent that does not exist. But `agent_names_claimed_by_docs()` splits the file at the `### Sub-agents this workflow depends on` heading and only scans below it.

The new section names all three agents above that heading:

```
`ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review` read more of the repository than the
change touches.
```

Rename or remove an agent and that line goes stale with the test green.

## Why it is minor

The guarded section would fail first on the same rename, so the failure is loud and the stale line gets found while fixing it. And the claim above the heading is only a *name*, not a capability — the class of thing #100 was filed about (prose asserting behaviour nothing enforces) is not what is unguarded here.

Worth fixing when the file is next touched rather than on its own.

## Options

1. Scan the whole file for agent-name references instead of the region below one heading. Straightforward, but it widens what the test treats as a claim — mentions in prose, examples and troubleshooting all become assertions.
2. Keep the region split and add a narrower whole-file check for backticked names matching a known agent-name shape.

(1) is probably right if the false-positive rate turns out to be low; worth counting the matches across the current file before deciding.

the repository sits on an old major with nothing to say so.

- `test_next_eslint_major_is_still_unsupported_upstream` measures the fact. It
  reads every `eslint` peer range declared in the web lockfile and fails once
  none of them caps below the next major -- the signal to delete the hold, close
  #69, and delete this module.
- `test_config_holds_the_eslint_major` measures the declaration, and only the
  declaration. It catches the hold being dropped while the block is still real,

## The conflict

AGENTS.md now says findings outside the current change get filed as issues, and that:

That depends on the sub-agent reporting them. But `.claude/agents/code-review.md` instructs the opposite:

So `code-review` is told to score pre-existing problems at 0 and discard them silently. The new AGENTS.md rule cannot reach anything `code-review` drops on that basis.

In practice the useful findings arrive anyway, because they come in under other headings — #151 surfaced as correctness at the seams, and the `sizes` mismatch in #152 as a pre-existing problem the change made materially worse. The rubric's filter is aimed at review *noise*, which is a real thing to suppress, and mostly it does that rather than suppressing genuine findings.

So this is a latent inconsistency, not an active defect. It matters because the new rule makes the sub-agents the primary discovery mechanism, and one of the three is told to discard a category the rule wants.

Is the right shape a separate, lower-weight channel — "not part of this change, but worth an issue" — distinct from the findings that block a commit? That would let `code-review` keep its noise filter for the blocking list while still surfacing what the workflow now wants captured.

"""Guard which Dependabot group a package lands in, for packages whose name lies.

`eslint-config-next` is published from the Next.js repository and carries Next's
version numbers. Its name says ESLint, and `eslint-*` in the `eslint` group's
patterns believed the name -- so it versioned with a family it does not belong
to, and inherited that family's blockers. While the ESLint 10 major was
unmergeable, #223 bundled the two into one pull request and neither could land;
`main` sat with `next` at 16.3.0 against `eslint-config-next` 16.2.12. That is
#252.

The assertion is on group *membership*, computed from the config's own patterns,
rather than on the presence of the lines that produce it. The two come apart in
both directions worth catching: an `exclude-patterns` entry can be dropped while
the explicit pattern below it stays, or a new group matching `eslint-*` can be
declared above `next` and take the package back without either existing line
changing. Grepping for either line reads as correct in both cases.

**This models Dependabot rather than running it**, which is the same compromise
`test_dependabot_holds.py` makes for npm resolution and states in its own
docstring: Dependabot's reading of this file is only observable from a Dependabot
run. Two documented rules are modelled here -- a dependency joins the first
group whose patterns match it, and `exclude-patterns` removes it from that
group's match set. `assert_model_matches_config_order` below is what stops the
model drifting into agreement with itself: it checks the group order the model
depends on against the file, so a reordering that would change the real answer
cannot leave the model silently reading a stale one.

`yaml` is deliberately not imported, for the reason `test_dependabot_holds.py`
gives: CI's script-test job builds a bare virtualenv, so a third-party import
passes locally and fails there.
"""

import fnmatch
import re
import unittest
from pathlib import Path

REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
DEPENDABOT_CONFIG = REPO_ROOT / ".github/dependabot.yml"

# The package this module exists for, and the group it belongs to.
PACKAGE = "eslint-config-next"
EXPECTED_GROUP = "next"


def update_entry(ecosystem: str, directory: str) -> list[str]:
    """The lines of one `updates:` entry, selected by ecosystem and directory."""
    lines = DEPENDABOT_CONFIG.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    starts = [i for i, line in enumerate(lines) if "- package-ecosystem:" in line]
    for position, start in enumerate(starts):
        end = starts[position + 1] if position + 1 < len(starts) else len(lines)
        entry = lines[start:end]
        body = "\n".join(entry)
        if f'package-ecosystem: "{ecosystem}"' in body and f'directory: "{directory}"' in body:
            return entry
    return []


def groups(entry: list[str]) -> list[tuple[str, list[str], list[str]]]:
    """Each group in declaration order, as (name, patterns, exclude_patterns).

    Order is carried rather than discarded because first-match-wins is the rule
    being modelled; a dict keyed by name would drop the one input the answer
    depends on.
    """
    out: list[tuple[str, list[str], list[str]]] = []
    inside = False
    name = ""
    key = ""
    patterns: list[str] = []
    excludes: list[str] = []

    def flush() -> None:
        if name:
            out.append((name, list(patterns), list(excludes)))

    for line in entry:
        if re.fullmatch(r"\s*groups:\s*", line):
            inside = True
            continue
        if not inside:
            continue
        # A key at the entry's own indentation ends the groups block.
        if line.strip() and not line.startswith("      "):
            break
        header = re.fullmatch(r"\s{6}([A-Za-z][\w-]*):\s*", line)
        if header:
            flush()
            name, key = header.group(1), ""
            patterns, excludes = [], []
            continue
        listing = re.fullmatch(r"\s{8}(patterns|exclude-patterns|update-types):\s*", line)
        if listing:
            key = listing.group(1)
            continue
        item = re.fullmatch(r'\s{10}-\s*"([^"]*)"\s*', line)
        if item and key == "patterns":
            patterns.append(item.group(1))
        elif item and key == "exclude-patterns":
            excludes.append(item.group(1))
    flush()
    return out


def group_for(package: str, declared: list[tuple[str, list[str], list[str]]]) -> str | None:
    """The first group whose patterns match `package` and whose excludes do not."""
    for name, patterns, excludes in declared:
        if any(fnmatch.fnmatchcase(package, pattern) for pattern in excludes):
            continue
        if any(fnmatch.fnmatchcase(package, pattern) for pattern in patterns):
            return name
    return None


class DependabotGroupingTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self) -> None:
        self.entry = update_entry("npm", "/apps/web")
        self.groups = groups(self.entry)

    def test_the_web_npm_entry_declares_groups(self):
        # Vacuity guard. Every assertion below passes against an empty list --
        # `group_for` returns None, and a mistyped indent or a renamed key would
        # produce exactly that while looking like a parse.
        self.assertTrue(self.entry, "no npm entry for /apps/web in dependabot.yml")
        self.assertGreaterEqual(len(self.groups), 5, f"parsed only {self.groups}")

    def test_eslint_config_next_versions_with_next(self):
        self.assertEqual(group_for(PACKAGE, self.groups), EXPECTED_GROUP)

    def test_eslint_group_still_claims_eslint_itself(self):
        # The exclude has to be narrower than the pattern it corrects. Excluding
        # `eslint-*` wholesale would satisfy the test above and quietly ungroup
        # every real ESLint plugin, which is the lockstep failure the grouping
        # exists to prevent.
        self.assertEqual(group_for("eslint", self.groups), "eslint")
        self.assertEqual(group_for("eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y", self.groups), "eslint")
        self.assertEqual(group_for("@typescript-eslint/parser", self.groups), "eslint")

    def test_next_itself_is_unaffected(self):
        self.assertEqual(group_for("next", self.groups), "next")
        self.assertEqual(group_for("@next/third-parties", self.groups), "next")

    def test_model_matches_the_declaration_order_it_depends_on(self):
        # The model's answer is only meaningful if `eslint` really is declared
        # before `next`; were that reversed, the exclude would be unnecessary and
        # this module would be asserting a rule the file no longer relies on.
        names = [name for name, _, _ in self.groups]
        self.assertIn("eslint", names)
        self.assertIn("next", names)
        self.assertLess(
            names.index("eslint"),
            names.index("next"),
            "`next` now precedes `eslint`; the exclude may be redundant -- recheck #252",
        )

def test_vitest_does_not_also_collect_the_journeys(self):
        """Playwright specs match vitest's default glob.

        Collected by vitest they fail on `@playwright/test` imports it cannot
        run, which reads as a broken unit suite rather than a config problem.

        The config is located rather than named. This read `vitest.config.ts`
        by hand until #281 renamed it to `.mts`, at which point it raised
        `FileNotFoundError` -- a stack trace about a missing path, rather than
        the exclusion being gone. Extensions here are enumerated rather than
        globbed because vitest writes `vitest.config.*.timestamp-*.mjs`
        alongside it while running, and a bare glob would count those.
        """
        candidates = [
            path
            for extension in ("ts", "mts", "cts", "js", "mjs", "cjs")
            if (path := REPO_ROOT / f"apps/web/vitest.config.{extension}").exists()
        ]
        # Vacuity guard: `assertIn` against a missing file cannot run at all,
        # and against two configs would pass on whichever came first while
        # vitest read the other.
        self.assertEqual(len(candidates), 1, f"expected one vitest config, found {candidates}")
        self.assertIn("e2e/**", candidates[0].read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

`eslint-config-next` is published from the Next.js repository and carries
Next's version numbers, but `eslint-*` in the `eslint` group matched it by
name and claimed it -- a dependency joins the first group whose patterns
match, and `eslint` is declared first.

That made it inherit a family's blockers rather than its own. While the
ESLint 10 major was held -- three packages peer-cap ESLint below 10, so
npm cannot install it -- #223 bundled the two into one unmergeable pull
request, and `main` sat with `next` at 16.3.0 against `eslint-config-next`
16.2.12.

with the exclude alone the package matches no later group until the
`npm-minor-patch` catch-all, so it detaches from `next` rather than
joining it; with the `next` pattern alone, `eslint` is declared first and
still claims it.

The guard asserts group *membership* computed from the config's own
patterns, not the presence of the lines that produce it. Those come apart
in both directions: an `exclude-patterns` entry can be dropped while the
pattern below it stays, and a new group matching `eslint-*` can be
declared above `next` and take the package back without either existing
line changing. Grepping for either line reads as correct in both cases.

It models Dependabot rather than running it, which is only observable
from a Dependabot run -- the same compromise `test_dependabot_holds.py`
documents for npm resolution. The rule is not taken on documentation
alone: `82c01ac` (#256) carries Dependabot's own trailer
`dependency-group: eslint` for `eslint-config-next`, so `eslint-*` really
did claim it, and it appeared in that group only though the catch-all's
`"*"` matches it too. Upstream changing those rules is the accepted
limit, stated in the module.

`update-types` is modelled rather than parsed and discarded. Without it
the model answers for a group Dependabot would skip: adding
`update-types: ["minor", "patch"]` to `next` decouples an
`eslint-config-next` major from `next` -- exactly the bump this pairing
exists for -- while every minor-bump assertion stays green.

`yaml` is not imported: CI's script-test job builds a bare virtualenv, so
a third-party import passes locally and fails there.

Both PRs are **CLEAN**. Here are my recommendations, and one of them changed once I looked at the code.

## #253 — take it, and it isn't your decision after all

I framed this as needing you to pick between three philosophies. It doesn't: **the repo already decided this exact question**, and the answer is sitting three lines above where the fix goes.

```python
    # Agent definitions are repo tooling. Without this they classify as
    # "unknown", which forces runtime by accident rather than by intent.
    ".claude/agents/**",
```

That is #253's option 3, already applied to an identical case. `RUNTIME_PATTERNS` also carries `.github/CODEOWNERS`, the PR template and the issue templates — none of which touch runtime code either. `changed_files_from_range` and `changed_files_from_worktree` in `scripts/detect_changed_surfaces.py` take git's path output literally. Git C-quotes any path containing a space or a non-ASCII byte, so those paths arrive wrapped in quotes and with escapes intact. Reproduced in a scratch repository:

```
$ git status --porcelain
 M "apps/web/a b.ts"
 M "apps/web/na\303\257ve.ts"
```

Both strings reach `matches_any` with the quoting attached. `apps/web/**` does not match `"apps/web/a b.ts"`, so an ordinary tracked source file classifies as `unknown`.

## Why it matters more than it looks

Routing fails in the safe direction — `unknown` forces the full runtime recommendation, so nothing is under-gated and no check is skipped. That is why it has never been visible.

The cost is to the flag rather than to the gate. `unknown` is supposed to mean "no pattern claims this path", and #253 has just narrowed it for exactly that reason: every classified file sheltering under the fallback makes the flag harder to tighten later without silently reclassifying whatever else was hiding there. A renamed component with a space in its filename reads, to that flag, as an unclassified path.

It also degrades the local loop more than CI. `make quick-ci-changed` uses the worktree path, so a developer working on such a file gets the full runtime target list rather than the web one, with no indication why.

## Fix

Pass `git -c core.quotePath=false` so non-ASCII comes through literally, and unquote the `"..."` form for the cases that remain (a literal quote, backslash, newline or tab in a filename still gets quoted regardless of `quotePath`).

`--porcelain=v1` documents the quoting rule; `-z` with NUL separators is the other standard answer and avoids the unquoting entirely, at the cost of changing how both readers split their output.

## Worth knowing when fixing

Both readers need it, not just one. `changed_files_from_range` feeds CI through `--base`/`--head`, and `changed_files_from_worktree` feeds `make quick-ci-changed`; the two take different git commands and only the second was exercised in the reproduction above.

A guard belongs with it — `tests/scripts/test_detect_changed_surfaces.py` already patches `run_git` for `test_changed_files_from_range_includes_deletions`, so a case returning a C-quoted path fits the existing shape.

Nothing checks that a requirement AGENTS.md places on a step is described in the agent that executes it

Found by `code-review` on `docs/workflow-guards-dpr-review-loop`, where it caught the first instance. Distinct from #153 and #154, so filing separately.

## The gap

`tests/scripts/test_agent_definitions.py` guards that AGENTS.md does not claim a sub-agent that does not exist, that the tool lists match, and that the step numbers line up. It does not check the **content** of a requirement.

So AGENTS.md can add an obligation to step 6, 7 or 8 that the agent performing that step is never told about, and `make test-scripts` stays green.

## The instance that found it

A step 6 addition required exercising UI-affecting changes at 2× device pixel ratio. `.claude/agents/ui-review.md` specified only three viewports, with no notion of density, and none of the tools it names sets `deviceScaleFactor` — that is a browser-context property, not a `browser_resize` argument. The runbook would have required something the executing agent was neither told to do nor pointed at a mechanism for.

Caught in review and fixed in the same change, by editing both files together. Nothing automated would have caught it.

## Why it matters more than it looks

The failure mode is quiet and specific: the agent does not refuse, it just does not do the thing, and reports the step complete. The caller reads a green step-6 report and believes the requirement was met. That is the same shape as #100, which is why the name and tool-list guards exist — this is the third face of it, after #153 (rubric versus filing) and #154 (name scanning below one heading).

## Hard to guard well

The obvious approach — assert that terms appearing in a step also appear in the executing agent's definition — is a keyword check, and would either miss paraphrase or fire on every ordinary word. Worth thinking about whether there is a cheaper structural answer:

- Keep the per-step obligations in one list that both AGENTS.md and the agent definitions are generated from or checked against.
- Or accept that this is a review-time concern rather than a test-time one, and put it in the reviewer's remit explicitly — a lighter fix, and honest about what a test can do here.

The second is probably right. Worth deciding rather than leaving it implied, since three separate issues now circle the same gap.

## What I claimed

That agent definitions are read once at session start, so editing one and invoking it in the same session gets the pre-edit version — making an agent-definition change unverifiable in the session that writes it.

## What is actually true

The definition an agent receives is the one **committed in `HEAD`**. The working tree is not read.

Four spawns of `ui-review`, each asked only whether a marker string appeared in its own instructions, with no file reads permitted:

| state of the definition | agent sees it |
| --- | --- |
| #287's probe rewrite, committed and merged mid-session | **yes** |

| same marker, still uncommitted, several minutes later | no |
| marker committed to `HEAD` | **yes** |
| marker still in `HEAD`, deleted from the working tree | **yes** |

The first row alone disproves the session-start claim: that change was made during this session and was picked up. The second and third rule out a short cache expiry. The fourth shows committing is what publishes it. The fifth shows the source is `HEAD` rather than the file on disk — the agent sees text that no longer exists in the working tree.

## What this means in practice

An agent-definition change **is** verifiable in the session that writes it. Commit it, then spawn the agent. No new session is needed.

The real trap is narrower and worse, because it sits exactly where this workflow spends its time: the review-fix loop. Commit, spawn the agent to verify, a reviewer finds a defect, edit the file — and that edit is invisible until it is committed again. Each round needs its own commit before the change under test is the change being tested. Amending is enough; the point is that `HEAD` has to move.

One observation, and a mechanism invented to explain it. A spawned `ui-review` quoted back a sentence I had just deleted — "Where the MCP server is **not connected**…" — and I concluded the definition was stale.

My grep for the deleted sentence used lowercase `not connected` and so did not match that bullet, and I took the absence of a match as proof the phrase was gone. The agent was almost certainly paraphrasing the new bullet, and I read a paraphrase as a verbatim quote.

That is the same error this repository keeps finding in my work: a real observation generalised past what it supports. Here it went into an issue, and from there into the record.

## The record it went into

The claim was repeated as fact in the commit bodies of #288 (`2f06de7`) and #299 (`040720b`), and in both pull request bodies, each saying the change could not be demonstrated in the session that wrote it. Both were committed before their pull requests opened, so both *were* demonstrable — the verification I said was impossible was available and I did not run it.

Leaving this issue open, re-scoped to the commit-visibility rule and the review-loop consequence, which is worth writing into `AGENTS.md` where anyone changing an agent will read it.

name: code-review
description: Reviews the current branch diff plus every staged, unstaged, and untracked file, as an expert in the languages and frameworks this repository uses. You review code for this repository before it is committed. You report findings. You never modify code, commit, or push.

## Operating rules

**Run without interaction.** No one is available to answer a question. Resolve ambiguity yourself, state the assumption, and continue. Never pause for confirmation.

**Never modify the repository.** No edits, no `git add`, no commits, no branch changes. If a fix seems obvious, describe it — the caller applies it.

**Precision over volume.** A review that buries two real bugs in fifteen nitpicks gets the bugs ignored. Report what a senior engineer on this codebase would actually stop the commit for.

## Scope

Review all of the following. The workflow requires it, and uncommitted work is exactly where accidental changes hide.

```bash
git diff main...HEAD          # committed on this branch
git diff                      # unstaged
git diff --cached             # staged
git status --short            # untracked
```

Read untracked files directly — they carry no diff. Also read enough surrounding code to judge each change in context; a diff alone hides callers, invariants, and prior art.

## What to look for

**Repository conventions.** `AGENTS.md` at the repo root, plus every nested runbook whose subtree the change touches — `apps/web/AGENTS.md`, `services/chat/AGENTS.md`, and `tests/scripts/AGENTS.md`. Read the ones covering the changed paths; each carries its own `## Code Review Rules`, and a scope you were never pointed at is a contract you cannot apply. Notable standing rules: pointer files (`CLAUDE.md`, `GEMINI.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`) must contain no instructions; Python runs from `.venv`; requirement manifests carry bare names with versions pinned in `constraints.txt`; hyphens not underscores in flag names; comments only where they carry real value.

**Bugs that will actually bite.** Logic errors, unhandled null and undefined, race conditions, incorrect async handling, resource leaks, security problems, N+1 queries and similar performance traps.

**Correctness at the seams.** This repository breaks most often where two systems meet rather than inside either one. Hand-written SQL against `apps/web/prisma/schema.prisma`. Files that must be copied into a container to exist at runtime. Dependency pins that must match a manifest entry. Web and chat request and response shapes that must agree. When a change touches one side of such a pair, check the other.

**Test quality.** Whether new tests would fail if the behaviour regressed. A test that passes against both the old and new implementation verifies nothing. Say so when you see one.

## Scoring and filtering

An edit under `.claude/agents/` reaches spawned agents after a **delay of a few minutes**. Not at session start, and not on commit.
